title: About 1,000 Edward Hospital Nurses in Naperville File for Union Election as Endeavor Health Plans Rush Merger
text:
About 1,000 Edward Hospital Nurses in Naperville File for Union Election as Endeavor Health Plans Rush Merger
About 1,000 registered nurses at Endeavor Health Edward Hospital in Naperville have asked federal labor officials to hold a union election. The petition filed with the National Labor Relations Board on Oct. 8 seeks representation by National Nurses United through its affiliate, the National Nurses Organizing Committee.
The filing comes as nurses at other Endeavor hospitals organize. On Oct. 14, Endeavor and Rush University System for Health also announced that they plan to merge. Together, the developments could reshape working conditions at one of the Chicago area's largest hospital networks.
For patients in DuPage County and the western suburbs, the main issue nurses raise is staffing, meaning how many patients each nurse cares for at once. No election date has been set.
Inside the Edward Hospital Petition
The proposed bargaining unit covers full-time, regular part-time, and per diem registered nurses at Edward's acute care hospital at 801 S. Washington St. in Naperville. It excludes nurses supplied by outside agencies or registries, nurse administrators, managers, and supervisors, according to NLRB records. The case is being handled by the agency's Region 13 office in Chicago, and Endeavor is represented by the law firm Ogletree Deakins, the records show.
Nurses say staffing and pay are driving the effort. Elizabeth Garcia, an intensive care nurse with 22 years at Edward, told the Daily Herald that she is sometimes assigned a third patient when units are full. "What we're really fighting (for) here is for safer working conditions, safer ratios," she said. Better pay and benefits are also on the nurses' list.
"We want to have a voice in patient care and be strong advocates for our patients and ourselves," said Amy Alaimo-Kruse, a nurse in Edward's women and children's float pool, in a National Nurses United news release.
Endeavor said it "respects the federally protected rights of our nurses to make an informed choice about union representation," the Daily Herald reported. The system also argued that a union acting as an intermediary could complicate safe, seamless patient care, and it emphasized direct collaboration between nurses and leaders.
Organizing Across the Endeavor System
Edward is the first Endeavor hospital where nurses have filed for an election, but it is not the only one where nurses are organizing. Nurses at Endeavor's Evanston, Skokie, Glenbrook, and Highland Park hospitals have been organizing with Teamsters Local 743, according to the Chicago Sun-Times. David Bernt, organizing director of Teamsters Joint Council 25, told the Daily Herald that the union believes it has enough support to move forward but gave no timeline for filing petitions.
The Teamsters have also filed NLRB charges alleging that two Evanston Hospital nurses were fired earlier this year because of their union activity, the Daily Herald reported. Endeavor did not comment directly on the firings, and the charges remain allegations.
Pay is another flashpoint. Tricia Poreda, a critical care resource nurse who works across the Evanston, Glenbrook, Skokie, and Highland Park hospitals, told the Daily Herald she saw a pay cut of $9 an hour after Endeavor cut nurse pay in 2025.
Nurses elsewhere in the region are taking similar steps. The National Nurses Organizing Committee has organized nearly 3,000 Chicago-area nurses over the past year, including at Rush University Medical Center, Olympia Fields Hospital, and Saint Mary of Nazareth Hospital, and now represents about 9,000 nurses in the area. Rush University Medical Center nurses voted to unionize with the committee in May, by a tally of 1,190 to 350.
Endeavor's finances add context. The nine-hospital system reported operating losses of $494 million in 2024 and $33.9 million in 2025. Most of the 2024 loss came from about $453 million in expenses to settle claims by patients who said a former OB-GYN sexually abused them.
What the Rush Merger Would Mean
The proposed merger would create a 12-hospital system in Chicago and its suburbs, operating under Rush. Endeavor's nine hospitals, which include Edward, Elmhurst, Evanston, Swedish, and Northwest Community, would keep their names and join Rush University Medical Center, Rush Copley Medical Center, and Rush Oak Park Hospital. The deal includes $1 billion from Endeavor's endowment for community programs, innovation, research, and academics.
J.P. Gallagher, Endeavor's current leader, would become president and CEO of the combined system. Rush President and CEO Dr. Omar Lateef would become CEO emeritus and a strategic adviser after the deal closes. Lateef said the merger could widen patient access to services such as clinical trials. "Nurses at Endeavor are vital to our mission; they're vital to our identity," Gallagher told the Sun-Times.
The merger still faces a regulatory review that could take months. It is unclear what it would mean for nurses seeking to unionize.
Union Vote Steps and Patient Care
The NLRB union election process follows set steps. A petition must show support from at least 30% of workers in the proposed unit, and the employer must post a notice telling employees that a petition was filed. Agency staff then confirm the board has jurisdiction and try to get both sides to agree on the election date, voting place, and who is eligible to vote. If they cannot agree, the regional director holds a hearing and may order an election.
A union wins if it receives a majority of the votes cast. Either side can file objections within seven days of the count, and the regional director's ruling can be appealed to the board in Washington. If certified, the union becomes the nurses' bargaining representative, and the hospital must bargain with it.
An election win would not by itself change staffing levels or pay. Those would depend on contract negotiations, which can take months or longer. Federal labor law also requires unions to give a health care facility at least 10 days' written notice before striking, which gives hospitals time to plan for patient care.
The petition itself does not affect scheduled care, and no strike has been called. Patients with concerns about staffing during a hospital stay can raise them with the charge nurse or the hospital's patient relations office, and they can report quality concerns to the Illinois Department of Public Health.
Key Questions Answered
What did Edward Hospital nurses file? About 1,000 registered nurses filed a petition with the National Labor Relations Board on Oct. 8 seeking a union election to join the National Nurses Organizing Committee, an affiliate of National Nurses United.
Why are the nurses organizing? Nurses cite staffing ratios, workloads, and pay. Endeavor says it respects their right to choose and prefers direct collaboration between nurses and leaders.
When will the union vote happen? No date has been set. NLRB staff will review the petition and try to get both sides to agree on election details.
Are nurses at other Endeavor hospitals unionizing? Nurses at the Evanston, Skokie, Glenbrook, and Highland Park hospitals have been organizing with Teamsters Local 743 but had not filed election petitions as of Oct. 13.
Will patient care at Edward Hospital change? The petition does not affect scheduled care, and no strike has been called. Any changes to staffing or pay would depend on future contract talks.
How does the Rush merger affect this? It is unclear. The proposed Endeavor and Rush merger faces a regulatory review that could take months.
